reviewer: AI source-based double-review; not external licensed pharmacist or legal certification; no psychometric validity claim

items.topic: Civil pharmacy negligence: limited prior-authorization notice duty versus Board discipline
items.legal_rule: Correa v. Schoeck, 479 Mass. 686, 694–702 (2018); Cottam v. CVS Pharmacy, 436 Mass. 316, 319–326 (2002); distinguish 247 CMR 10.03 Board discipline
items.distinct_decision: Novelty vs E30-096/101/161/201: asks about a specific MA Supreme Judicial Court civil duty in insurance PA communication, not automatic Board sanction; original exam-style case, not recalled content.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Correa expressly rejected an open-ended duty to ensure that the physician received and acted on a PA request; the duty is to take reasonable notification steps, not to guarantee insurer coverage or prescriber response.

Correct. In Correa v. Schoeck, 479 Mass. 686 (2018), the SJC recognized a limited duty to take reasonable steps to notify the patient and prescribing clinician of a PA barrier at each attempted fill; no universal duty to obtain the insurer's approval was imposed.

Incorrect. The specific PA communication duty recognized in Correa is a counterexample. A payment rejection is not an automatic blanket exemption from reasonable patient/prescriber notice, particularly where a serious treatment gap is known.

Correct. Civil negligence and professional license discipline are separate processes. The SJC's limited duty analysis does not depend on a Board conviction, but proving duty alone does not establish compensable negligence without breach and injury caused by it.

items.topic: Limited-English-proficiency counseling: interpreter access and HIPAA
items.legal_rule: 45 CFR 92.201(a)–(c) (meaningful access; qualified language assistance); 45 CFR 164.506(c) (HIPAA TPO); HHS OCR Section 1557 language-access guidance
items.distinct_decision: Tests LEP access and interpreter privacy, distinct from E30-003/092/137 delegation of counseling and alternative contact.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. 45 CFR 92.201 requires meaningful, timely, accurate, no-cost language assistance in covered health programs. An appropriate qualified interpreter can facilitate counseling while protecting confidentiality; HIPAA generally permits provider use of interpreters for treatment or health care operations.

Incorrect. Section 1557's language-access protections generally prohibit reliance on accompanying minors for interpreting except narrowly defined exigent circumstances; convenience and assumed fluency do not establish qualified medical interpretation.

Incorrect. Section 1557's required language assistance must be free of charge to the individual with limited English proficiency. Drug insurance coverage does not transfer this accessibility cost to the patient.

Incorrect. Qualified interpretation requires accuracy, impartiality, relevant terminology and privacy safeguards. Being conversationally bilingual is not a categorical substitute for qualified healthcare interpretation.

items.topic: Controlled substance office stock disguised as patient prescription
items.legal_rule: 21 CFR 1306.04(a)–(b) (legitimate medical purpose; prohibition on Rx for office stock); 21 CFR 1306.05(a) (patient information); 21 CFR Part 1305 for qualifying Schedule II registrant orders
items.distinct_decision: Differs from E30-024 pharmacy-to-pharmacy five-percent distribution and E30-178 patient-specific red flags; physician is buying general office stock rather than treating a named patient.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. A practitioner's valid DEA registration does not turn general office inventory into a patient-specific prescription. 21 CFR 1306.04(b) explicitly prohibits using an individual-practitioner prescription to obtain stock for future general dispensing.

Incorrect. Relabeling the clinic's planned office stock as a personal prescription would not create a legitimate patient-specific order. Documented intent still remains supply for general office dispensing.

Incorrect. A prescription must be legitimate at issuance and bear required patient information; a month-end accounting cannot retroactively convert a general stock replenishment into lawful patient-specific prescribing.

Correct. 21 CFR 1306.04(b) prohibits an individual practitioner issuing a controlled prescription to supply general dispensing stock. If the practitioner may lawfully acquire stock, that requires appropriate registrant purchasing or transfer processes rather than a disguised retail prescription.

items.topic: Poison Prevention Packaging Act: product exceptions versus patient waiver
items.legal_rule: 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10)(i),(iv) (special-packaging exemptions); 16 CFR 1701.1 and PPPA consumer/prescriber conventional-packaging requests; CPSC Healthcare Professional Guide (2023)
items.distinct_decision: Unlike E30-029, tests expressly exempt product/package types rather than carrying forward a patient-specific child-resistant waiver.
items.planned_skill_changed: Replaced proposed additional Schedule V classification with PPPA product-specific exemptions vs prior waiver.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10) expressly excepts specified products, including sublingual nitroglycerin and qualifying cyclic hormonal contraceptives in manufacturer mnemonic dispensers.

Correct. Section 1700.14(a)(10)(i) exempts sublingual nitroglycerin; (iv) exempts certain cyclically administered contraceptives in manufacturers' mnemonic packages. An otherwise covered ordinary oral antibiotic remains subject to special-packaging requirements absent a valid exception.

Incorrect. The cited cyclic contraceptive exception is tied to a qualifying manufacturer's mnemonic dispenser and specified hormone activity; it does not convert all repackaged contraceptive tablets into a blanket exemption.
Incorrect. The pharmacist cannot unilaterally replace PPPA-compliant packaging simply for convenience. A qualifying request or specific product-based exception is needed under the PPPA.

items.topic: DEA pharmacy closure/ownership transfer: registration and controlled-stock records
items.legal_rule: 21 CFR 1301.52(a)–(b),(d)(1)–(2); 21 CFR 1304.11 (inventory); 21 CFR Part 1305 (Schedule II orders); 247 CMR 6.11 (separate MA pharmacy ownership process)
items.distinct_decision: Novel DEA final/initial inventory and 14-day business-transfer reporting compared with E30-065 MA facility licensing and E30-180 reverse distributor destruction.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Under 21 CFR 1301.52(d), a registrant discontinuing controlled business by transferring stock to another person generally submits prescribed information to the local Special Agent in Charge at least 14 days in advance unless this period is waived.
Incorrect. A financial asset valuation does not replace the mandatory complete controlled-substance inventory required at the transfer, nor does it satisfy the required registrant records.

Correct. Section 1301.52(d)(1)-(2) uses the on-transfer inventory for both registrants and directs Schedule I–II transfers to Part 1305 order forms, in addition to transferring the required controlled-substance records.

Incorrect. Under §1301.52(a)-(b), DEA registration does not automatically transfer to a different legal registrant. DEA authority must independently support the acquiring registrant's operations; name or MOR continuity is not a substitute.

items.topic: Technician immunization authorization: biennial continuing training
items.legal_rule: Massachusetts Board Policy 2023-02, revised September 4, 2025, §III(D)(1)–(5): initial qualifications and two-hour immunization CE/updated training every two years
items.distinct_decision: Unlike E30-062/191, tests continued eligibility after initial training rather than 500 post-license work hours or vaccine selection.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Policy 2023-02 establishes a biennial immunization education/update requirement, not an automatic reset of the technician licensure/training-employment pathway after two years.

Incorrect. National technician certification and CPR are separate prerequisites. The policy expressly adds periodic immunization-specific education or updated training regardless of those other credentials.

Correct. Revised Policy 2023-02, §III(D)(5), requires at least two hours of immunization-related continuing education or updated training every two years. The prior initial six-hour program and two on-the-job hours do not substitute for maintaining this ongoing requirement.

Incorrect. Supervising-pharmacist clinical oversight does not create an exception to the Board's specified two-hours-every-two-years requirement. Reviewing past injections alone is not the stated education or updated training.

items.topic: Community CDTM: adding a different diagnosis to an individual referral
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)(1)–(4),(d),(e)(1)(b)(ix),(e)(3)–(4); 247 CMR 16.04(1) (patient-specific referral/consent and community CDTM prescriptive limits)
items.distinct_decision: Distinct from E30-036 diabetes dose modification already under a diabetes-specific referral; tests a new diagnosis absent from the individual referral.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Under 247 CMR 16.03(5)(c)(2), the supervising physician must specify each primary and secondary diagnosis in the written patient referral or a subsequent referral. Community-CDTM prescribing for comorbidities additionally must be authorized in the patient referral.

Incorrect. The community pathway requires the physician's individual referral to specify the patient's primary and secondary diagnoses; a broad agreement listing diabetes does not automatically make the patient referred for that condition.
Incorrect. The patient-specific referral cannot extend community CDTM prescribing beyond the authorized Schedule VI scope under 247 CMR 16.03(5), even when a physician is aware of the new condition.

Correct. Sections 16.03(5)(c)-(d) and 16.04(1) require patient-specific written informed consent and defined distribution/record custody. The physician retains the original and transmits a copy to the pharmacist within 24 hours.

items.topic: PDMA practitioner sample distribution versus retail-pharmacy resale
items.legal_rule: 21 CFR 203.30(a)(1)–(4),(b)–(c), 203.31(a) (PDMA drug sample requests and receipts); 247 CMR 9.01(6) (sample resale/compounding/repackaging restriction)
items.distinct_decision: Unlike E30-132, which tests illegal pharmacy resale of samples, tests the authorized clinician-request sample supply chain and recipient records.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Federal PDMA rules recognize the licensed-practitioner request and hospital-pharmacy recipient with documented receipt. Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.01(6) separately prohibits pharmacies accepting/purchasing samples for compounding, repacking, or reselling them.

Incorrect. 21 CFR 203.30–203.31 expressly permit qualifying manufacturer or authorized-distributor shipments to a hospital or other healthcare-entity pharmacy at a licensed practitioner's written request when verification, delivery receipt and other rules are met.
Incorrect. The signed receipt provides required traceability and confirmation of sample delivery; it does not authorize selling products marked as drug samples not for resale.

Incorrect. 21 CFR 203.30(a) imposes an advance signed written request, verification of the requester's prescriptive authority, and a written recipient receipt returned to the manufacturer or distributor, among other requirements.

items.topic: Unfilled electronic CII transfer: direct licensed-pharmacist communication and electronic annotations
items.legal_rule: MA Board Policy 2023-10 I–II (Unfilled Prescriptions); 21 CFR 1306.08(e)–(h) (initial-fill EPCS transfer, documentation, retention); 247 CMR 9.14
items.distinct_decision: Compared with E30-007 generic permission to transfer unfilled Rx, tests conversion prohibition, licensed-pharmacist actor, annotations and bilateral records.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Federal 21 CFR 1306.08(f)(1) requires an EPCS initial-fill transfer to stay in electronic prescription form; a PDF, email document or fax intermediary is not lawful conversion of that electronic prescription.

Incorrect. Section 1306.08(f)(3) requires communication directly between TWO licensed pharmacists for the controlled initial-fill transfer. Massachusetts technician authority for Schedule VI transfers does not extend to Schedule II EPCS.
Incorrect. 21 CFR 1306.08(f)(4)-(h) requires specified annotations at both transferring and receiving pharmacies and retention of electronic transfer records by both for two years.

Correct. Massachusetts Policy 2023-10 adopts 21 CFR 1306.08(e)-(h) for unfilled Schedule II–V EPCS. The electronic prescription stays intact, both pharmacists communicate directly, required dates/DEA IDs/names are annotated and retained at both pharmacies.

items.topic: After 2026 viable-air action result: repeat EM and normal BUD restoration
items.legal_rule: MA Board Policy 2026-03 §IV(A)–(C), especially IV(B)(1)–(3), Environmental Monitoring action level response (adopted September 3, 2026); USP <797> applicable EM standards
items.distinct_decision: This asks how to establish successful remediation and RESTORE normal BUDs, rather than E30-160 initial ISO7 excursion treatment or E30-215 ISO5 18CFU initial recall. Board policy directly verified; subscribed USP full text not represented as accessed.
items.source_limitations: MA Board 2026-03 corroborates EM; subscribed USP-NF text not directly inspected

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Under §IV(B)(2), restoration of standard BUDs depends on repeat EM falling below action levels; deep cleaning alone, particularly a sample collected immediately after cleaning, is not accepted proof of sustained control.

Correct. Policy 2026-03 §IV(B)(1) permits repeat EM focused on the affected classified area/type as supported by the monitoring plan, but requires all sampling locations within that affected area to be re-sampled simultaneously.

Correct. Policy §IV(B)(2) expressly allows restoration of standard BUDs or resumption of compounding when repeat EM is below action levels, subject to compliance with otherwise applicable sterile standards.

Incorrect. Section IV(B)(3) sends repeated action-level results back to §III response duties. A smaller but still above-threshold CFU reading is not clearance and cannot automatically support normal BUDs.

items.topic: Pharmacist continuing education audit: proof and retention
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 4.06(1)–(2) (CE completion records retained at least two years and provided on audit); Board Policy 2021-04 §I (most recent two full calendar years; non-ACPE certificate details)
items.distinct_decision: Tests authentic CE records on random audit, not E30-201 deliberate fabrication or E30-146 compounding specialty hour quota.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Board Policy 2021-04 recognizes certain non-ACPE credits but requires the pharmacist to retain sufficient completion documentation when the education does not appear in CPE Monitor; the Board may request those records.

Correct. 247 CMR 4.06(1)-(2) requires documentation or statements of credit containing the specified identifying details, maintained at least two years from completion and submitted on Board request/random audit. Policy 2021-04 further describes evidence expected for non-ACPE activity.
Incorrect. An unauthenticated calendar entry showing only a seminar title does not demonstrate successful completion or identify all required provider, participant, activity, date and credit details.
Incorrect. Section 4.06(2) expressly permits random audits and Board requests for documentation independent of the moment of renewal.

items.topic: 42 CFR Part 2 intermediary: patient request for disclosure recipient list
items.legal_rule: 42 CFR 2.24(a)–(b) (specific intermediary's 30-day response and 3-year request); contrast 42 CFR 2.25 and HHS 2024 Part 2 final-rule fact sheet (accounting compliance-date caveat)
items.distinct_decision: Distinct from E30-028 consent/SUD notes and E30-203 notice/fundraising; narrower intermediary-rights rule avoids treating the deferred general accounting implementation as effective.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. The list requirement specifically protects patients who used general-designation consents; prior consent does not waive their ability to learn who received information under that designation.
Correct. Under 42 CFR 2.24(b)(1), an intermediary named on the general-designation consent must respond in 30 or fewer days after receiving the qualifying written request.

Incorrect. The narrow §2.24 intermediary list is not the broader §2.25 electronic-health-record accounting right. HHS has stated that the §2.25 accounting compliance date depends on the separate HIPAA accounting rule update; the two rights should not be conflated.
Correct. Section 2.24(a) limits the written request to the previous three years and §2.24(b)(2) specifies recipient entity name(s), date and a brief description of identifying information.

items.topic: Lenalidomide REMS: expired pharmacy confirmation number
items.legal_rule: FDA-approved Lenalidomide REMS Pharmacy Guide, steps 3–4: valid 24-hour pharmacy confirmation, cancellation/reissue when expired, Medication Guide; 247 CMR 9.01(21) (comply with product REMS)
items.distinct_decision: Specific current program source: https://www.lenalidomiderems.com/media/wp-content/uploads/LEN_Pharmacy_Guide.pdf. Distinct from E30-063 isotretinoin windows and E30-183 esketamine REMS site administration.
items.source_limitations: Current sponsor REMS guide, not a case-specific completion of REMS authorization

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. The active Lenalidomide REMS pharmacy procedures state that a confirmation number is valid for only 24 hours. When it has expired, the pharmacy must cancel the old number and obtain a new one before dispensing while complying with the remaining REMS safeguards.
Incorrect. The Lenalidomide REMS Pharmacy Guide limits a pharmacy confirmation number's validity to 24 hours. A confirmation obtained 26 hours earlier is no longer sufficient for dispensing.

Incorrect. A REMS is a distribution/safe-use restriction, not a controlled-schedule exception. Lenalidomide REMS independently requires confirmation before each dispensing and does not allow ordinary automatic refills.
Incorrect. A prescriber countersignature cannot extend the 24-hour program confirmation; pharmacist certification also does not cancel the Medication Guide and patient-counseling requirements.

items.topic: Massachusetts generic interchange: special container label and manufacturer
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.05(3)(a)–(e), generic/brand interchange container label and abbreviations; M.G.L. c.112 §12D (interchange authority)
items.distinct_decision: Not E30-194 missing pharmacist initials or E30-019 whether interchange is required; tests exact label identifying actual substituted product and manufacturer.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Section 9.05(3)(a) specifically requires the label to identify the actual generic product and its manufacturer in an interchange statement; showing only the prescribed brand would not communicate what was dispensed.
Incorrect. Therapeutic interchangeability authorizes selection under applicable circumstances but does not waive the separate container labeling obligation in §9.05(3).

Correct. Section 9.05(3)(a),(c)-(d) requires the 'Interchange' generic name/manufacturer presentation for a less expensive dispensed generic and permits recognized abbreviations, e.g. 'IC', plus an optional 'for [prescribed brand]' notation.
Incorrect. Section 9.05(3)(d) expressly allows commonly understood abbreviations, including 'IC' and recognized abbreviations for manufacturer names.

items.topic: Hospital nursing-unit controlled-stock accountability and witnessed waste
items.legal_rule: Massachusetts DPH General Accountability Guidelines for Controlled Substances in Hospitals and Clinics with Pharmacies, Nursing Units—General and Schedule II–V; 105 CMR 700.005 (security and accountability); 247 CMR 9.12 (separate institutional ADD)
items.distinct_decision: Explicitly tests documented nursing-unit stock security and waste, not E30-155 patient-specific order authorization for a hospital automated dispensing device. DPH guidance is identified as guidance rather than represented as independently enacted regulation.
items.source_limitations: Massachusetts DPH hospital accountability operational guidance, not an enacted new 247 CMR obligation

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Massachusetts DPH's nursing-unit accountability guidance states that Schedule II–V controlled drugs must be in a double-locked, permanently affixed unit/cart with perpetual inventory records.
Incorrect. The DPH guidance restricts controlled-substance access to licensed, authorized staff; familiarity or visitor trust does not replace controlled inventory security.
Correct. The state DPH accountability guidance specifies two licensed staff and co-signature for disposal of unused Schedule II–V portions, subject to stricter facility policy.
Incorrect. DPH calls for a documented quality-assurance review of controlled substances administered on nursing units not less than once weekly; an access log does not replace the management review.

items.topic: Graduating pharmacist: initial-calendar-year CE exemption versus following year's requirements
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 4.03(4),(5),(8) (annual CE, no carryover and graduation-year exception); Massachusetts Board Policy 2021-04 general compliance (revised Sep. 4, 2025)
items.distinct_decision: Novel graduate-year CE exception under §4.03(8). Replaced an almost duplicate PGY1-resident intern case already tested in E30-076. Differs from E30-226 proof and retention of CE credits.
items.planned_skill_changed: Replaced duplicate PharmD residency intern status already in E30-076 with a graduation-calendar-year CE exception.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Section 4.03(8) expressly exempts a registrant from continuing education in the calendar year the registrant graduated from an approved pharmacy school; obtaining licensure that same year does not remove the exemption.
Incorrect. The regulatory exception is tied to the specific calendar year of graduation. It is not a two-year rolling extension of the annual CE requirement into 2027.

Correct. 247 CMR 4.03(8) exempts the pharmacist from CE in the 2026 graduation calendar year. Section 4.03(4)-(5) imposes yearly CE requirements afterward and disallows carrying prior-year contact hours into the next calendar year. Other practice-specific CE would be analyzed separately if relevant.
Incorrect. Section 4.03(5) expressly disallows carrying contact hours between calendar years. Extra activity during an exempt graduation year does not prepay a later calendar year's requirements.

items.topic: MIIS pre-vaccination lookup: influenza versus zoster and COVID-19
items.legal_rule: Board Policy 2023-02 §§IV(E)–(G), revised September 4, 2025; 105 CMR 222.100(A) (MIIS immunization reporting)
items.distinct_decision: Does not repeat E30-037 patient's MIIS data-sharing objection or E30-093 federal VIS/record fields; focuses on influenza/COVID-19 exception vs zoster mandatory precheck.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Section IV(F) RECOMMENDS checking earlier COVID-19 vaccine formulation and dates and recognizes MIIS, pharmacy/EHR records or the vaccination card; that is not the identical mandatory pre-lookup rule used for zoster.

Incorrect. Section IV(G) requires pharmacy personnel to report administered vaccination information to MIIS, and 105 CMR 222.100 generally imposes a 72-hour reporting duty. A lookup exception is not a reporting waiver.

Correct. Policy 2023-02 §IV(E) requires reviewing MIIS before vaccines OTHER THAN influenza or COVID-19. The exemption is to that particular pre-administration lookup, not to the separate vaccine-record reporting requirements.
Correct. The zoster vaccine is not one of the influenza/COVID-19 exceptions listed in §IV(E); the pharmacy must review MIIS in advance under the Board's vaccination policy.

items.topic: 2026 Part 2 unsecured SUD-record breach notification under HIPAA-equivalent rule
items.legal_rule: 42 CFR 2.16(b) (Part 2 unsecured-record breach adopts HIPAA Breach Rule); 45 CFR 164.404(b) (individual notices), 164.408(c) (under-500 Secretary annual report); HHS OCR Part 2 breach guidance (compliance February 16, 2026)
items.distinct_decision: E30-033 tests exactly-500 HIPAA breach media boundary; E30-073 tests encryption/compromise risk. This scenario tests Part 2 applicability to a 120-patient unsecured SUD record breach after February 2026.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. The HIPAA-equivalent breach rules apply to Part 2 records. The 500-person threshold changes some Secretary/media notification timing, but does not eliminate the obligation to notify affected patients of an actual breach.

Incorrect. Part 2's confidentiality protections do not prohibit the specific notifications required by §2.16(b). An appropriately handled qualified service organization does not replace individual breach notices.

Incorrect. Part 2 independently establishes breach notification obligations even for programs not otherwise HIPAA covered; a Board pharmacy-reporting clock does not replace Part 2's HHS/individual notifications.

Correct. 42 CFR 2.16(b) applies HIPAA Breach Notification Rule requirements. 45 CFR 164.404 requires individual notification without unreasonable delay and within 60 calendar days, while §164.408(c) permits the annual HHS report for breaches affecting fewer than 500 people within 60 days after the end of the calendar year.

items.topic: Automatic-refill program: patient enrollment consent and opt-out
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.19(13) (patient/agent recorded consent before auto-refill enrollment; discontinuation method); 247 CMR 9.04(12) (separate Schedule VI prescription validity)
items.distinct_decision: Under-tested patient-choice automatic-refill practice, distinct from E30-084 transferring remaining refills and E30-089 unclaimed return-to-stock.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Section 9.19(13) requires prior recorded patient/agent consent and a mechanism to end participation in an automatic refill program. Refill validity and amount remain independently governed by prescription laws.

Incorrect. Prescription refill authorization from the prescriber and patient agreement to participate in pharmacy AUTOMATION are separate matters. §9.19(13) expressly requires obtaining and recording patient/agent consent before enrollment.
Incorrect. Section 9.19(13) recognizes a patient's ability to stop the program. Participating in auto-refill is not an additional legal prerequisite to otherwise authorized ordinary refills.
Incorrect. Auto-refill consent cannot extend the legal issuance/refill validity of the underlying Schedule VI prescription under 247 CMR 9.04(12).

items.topic: Workplace prescription collection and direct handoff: lawful pharmacy-agent workflow
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.04(9)(a)–(e) (collection at industrial plants/workplaces, eligible recipients, direct handoff and undistributed return)
items.distinct_decision: Distinct from E30-110 failed mail delivery with temperature excursion and E30-138 inpatient bedside-delivery consent. Tests workplace direct custody and pharmacy-agent accountability.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Section 9.04(9)(a) allows this particular workplace/group-affiliation collection pathway only for persons regularly employed/affiliated or their immediate family members residing at the same address.

Correct. Sections 9.04(9)(b)-(c) require in-person collection by an authorized pharmacy representative and direct handoff of filled medications to the patient or agent. A generic employer mailroom drop does not satisfy this narrow program.
Incorrect. Section 9.04(9)(c)-(d) requires direct dispensing to the patient or agent and the return of medication not directly dispensed; medications may not be left or stored at the workplace.
Incorrect. Section 9.04(9)(e) expressly holds the pharmacy and pharmacist responsible for conduct of the pharmacy employee or authorized agent acting on their behalf.

items.topic: New staff licensure verification: pharmacy responsibility at commencement of employment
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.19(18) (current licensure verification at commencement for pharmacist, intern, technician and trainee); 247 CMR 8.03 (pharmacy technician trainee licensure and scope); 247 CMR 9.04(1) (pharmacist final validation)
items.distinct_decision: Different from E30-121 (national certification lapse but continued valid Massachusetts technician license) and E30-156 (expired pharmacist's individual practice); new decision is the EMPLOYING pharmacy's commencement-date verification of every credentialed class.
items.planned_skill_changed: Replaced duplicate national-technician-certification lapse E30-121 with the employer's current-licensure verification at hiring.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.19(18) makes verification of CURRENT licensure at the commencement of employment a pharmacy obligation. A historic screening months earlier does not excuse checking the worker's status on arrival.

Correct. The pharmacy must verify licensure status upon commencement for pharmacists, interns, technicians and technician trainees under §9.19(18). An expired trainee license cannot be treated as active during application processing; restrict duties until a valid credential is confirmed.

Incorrect. The same current-license verification duty expressly includes technician trainees. A technician's training-hour eligibility limits do not create permission to work before obtaining or renewing the requisite trainee license.
Incorrect. Computer checks and pharmacist supervision do not cure an expired individual credential or create authority to handle prohibited controlled-substance inventory.

items.topic: Schedule VI prescription continuity supply after expired prescription or zero authorized refills
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.04(12) (MA Schedule VI one-year validity and narrow 14-day/smallest-unit-of-use emergency continuity supply); compare 247 CMR 9.04(13) and 21 CFR 1306.22 for federal CIII–V
items.distinct_decision: New short-quantity continuity decision not previously tested in the 215 originals; current 2024 regulation says 14 days, NOT the 30 days in an older inspection-template excerpt.
items.planned_skill_changed: Replaced inaccessible state PrEP restart protocol candidate with 247 CMR 9.04(12) Schedule VI continuity supply.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. The narrowly defined 14-day or smallest-available-unit-of-use limit controls; historical adherence does not confer unlimited extension of a stale prescription.

Correct. Current 247 CMR 9.04(12) expressly authorizes pharmacist-judgment dispensing of up to 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use package when a Schedule VI prescription is expired or lacks refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained promptly.

Correct. Subsection 9.04(12) explicitly addresses expired/no-refill Schedule VI cases and grants a separate narrow dispensing pathway when timely prescriber authorization cannot be obtained. The pharmacist must still use professional judgment.

Incorrect. Section 9.04(12) is written specifically for Massachusetts Schedule VI. A federally controlled Schedule IV refill is subject to its separate federal and state rules and cannot be extended merely by importing this Schedule VI exception.

items.topic: Veterinarian federal Schedule III prescriptive authorization vs Schedule VI-only registration
items.legal_rule: M.G.L. c.94C §§7,18(a); 105 CMR 700.004(C)–(D) (MCSR schedule authorizations); DEA 21 CFR 1306.03–1306.05; Massachusetts DPH Veterinary Prescriptions Best Practice Recommendations (January 9, 2025)
items.distinct_decision: Contrast E30-208, where veterinarian has lawful VI MCSR to prescribe ordinary amoxicillin without a DEA number. This one tests missing federally scheduled III authority after a genuine animal exam.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. Veterinarian status does not grant blanket exemption from federal controlled-substance registration for Schedule II–V prescribing. Massachusetts DPH specifically distinguishes DEA registration for Schedules II–V from Schedule VI-only MCSR authority.

Incorrect. The patient is an animal being treated within a legitimate veterinarian-client-patient relationship. Rewriting the patient does not create DEA prescribing authority and can make the prescription fictitious.

Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §§7,18 and 105 CMR 700.004 require appropriate registrations/schedule authorization; DEA registration is needed for federally scheduled III drugs. The same veterinarian could prescribe lawful Schedule VI-only products under the narrower Massachusetts MCSR if other conditions are met.
Incorrect. Refill rules do not make an order valid when the practitioner lacks required authority for the federal controlled schedule at issuance.

items.topic: MassPAT additional drug gabapentin: positive identification and hardship exception
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.04(14)(a)–(d) (positive identification for Schedules II–V and 'additional drugs', documented serious-hardship alternative); 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) (gabapentin additional-drug reporting)
items.distinct_decision: Different from E30-005 Schedule II hardship-only case and E30-039 MassPAT reporting without physical pickup ID; integrates the additional-drug patient identity rule.

option_verdicts.basis: Incorrect. DPH designated gabapentin an additional PMP-reportable drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). Section 9.04(14) expressly extends positive identification to such additional drugs even though they are Massachusetts Schedule VI.

Correct. Section 9.04(14)(b)-(c) generally requires customer positive identification for PMP additional drugs. The specific alternative permits dispensing where denial would cause serious hardship, provided the justification is documented and the ultimate user or agent writes the specified information and signs.
Incorrect. Section 9.04(14)(c) expressly covers both federal Schedule II–V products AND additional drugs in its documented serious-hardship alternative.

Incorrect. Customer identification concerns the actual ultimate user or agent presenting the prescription. Someone else's ID does not satisfy the rule, and a hardship-based dispensing requires the specific signed log and documented reason.

items.topic: Ransomware downtime: pharmacy continuity procedures, patient profiles and DUR records
items.legal_rule: 247 CMR 9.19(22)(a)–(d) (mandatory pharmacy computer downtime plan), 9.16(1),(7) (record retention/confidential profile), 9.17(1)–(2) (prospective DUR); HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR 164.308–312 separately governs covered electronic PHI
items.distinct_decision: Ransomware is the scenario; exact binding action tested is the Board's computer downtime continuity, profile reconciliation and DUR SOP, not a speculative cyber breach report deadline. Distinct from E30-085 controlled record segregation.

option_verdicts.basis: Correct. Section 9.19(22)(a)-(b) requires a downtime policy that includes a lawful filling process and later incorporation into the computerized pharmacy patient record. A breach does not eliminate the documentation/reconciliation obligation.

Incorrect. Section 9.19(22)(d) requires an appropriate DUR process during downtime, and §9.17 keeps pharmacist prospective DUR obligations in force. A computerized alert is a tool, not a substitute for pharmacist judgment.

Incorrect. Falsifying or deleting records to conceal the incident violates pharmacy recordkeeping duties and undermines lawful traceability. Downtime procedures call for accurate reconciliation, not fabrication or erasure.

Correct. Sections 9.16–9.17 require confidential, retrievable patient records and appropriate prospective review. The downtime plan must preserve continuity and ensure eventual patient-profile entry, without pretending records are currently accessible if they are not.

quality_corrections.details: Eleven correct option texts were condensed while preserving regulatory claims, exact answer keys and each option's legal explanation. Four SBA correct choices remain longest, one shortest, ten intermediate; revised existing first 215 unchanged.
